vulnerability.title: Disable Bluetooth Kernel Module
vulnerability.description: The kernel's module loading system can be configured to prevent loading of the Bluetooth module. Add the following to the appropriate /etc/modprobe.d configuration file to prevent the loading of the Bluetooth module: install bluetooth /bin/true
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then if LC_ALL=C grep -q -m 1 "^install bluetooth" /etc/modprobe.d/bluetooth.conf ; then sed -i 's#^install bluetooth.*#install bluetooth /bin/false#g' /etc/modprobe.d/bluetooth.conf else echo -e "\n# Disable per security requirements" >> /etc/modprobe.d/bluetooth.conf echo "install bluetooth /bin/false" >> /etc/modprobe.d/bluetooth.conf fi if ! LC_ALL=C grep -q -m 1 "^blacklist bluetooth$" /etc/modprobe.d/bluetooth.conf ; then echo "blacklist bluetooth" >> /etc/modprobe.d/bluetooth.conf fi else >&2 echo 'Remediation is not applicable, nothing was done' fi

vulnerability.description: The DNS processing mode in NetworkManager describes how DNS is processed on the system. Depending the mode some changes the system's DNS may not be respected.
vulnerability.recommendation:
Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q NetworkManager; then var_networkmanager_dns_mode='' found=false # set value in all files if they contain section or key for f in $(echo -n "/etc/NetworkManager/conf.d/complianceascode_hardening.conf /etc/NetworkManager/conf.d/*.conf /etc/NetworkManager/NetworkManager.conf"); do if [ ! -e "$f" ]; then continue fi # find key in section and change value if grep -qzosP "[[:space:]]*\[main\]([^
\[]*
+)+?[[:space:]]*dns" "$f"; then if ! grep -qPz "dns=$var_networkmanager_dns_mode" "$f"; then sed -i "s/dns[^(
)]*/dns=$var_networkmanager_dns_mode/" "$f" fi found=true # find section and add key = value to it elif grep -qs "[[:space:]]*\[main\]" "$f"; then sed -i "/[[:space:]]*\[main\]/a dns=$var_networkmanager_dns_mode" "$f"

vulnerability.title: Disable Modprobe Loading of USB Storage Driver
vulnerability.description: To prevent USB storage devices from being used, configure the kernel module loading system to prevent automatic loading of the USB storage driver. To configure the system to prevent the usb-storage kernel module from being loaded, add the following line to the file /etc/modprobe.d/usb-storage.conf: install usb-storage /bin/false This entry will cause a non-zero return value during a usb-storage module installation and additionally convey the meaning of the entry to the user in form of an error message. If you would like to omit a non-zero return value and an error message, you may want to add a different line instead (both /bin/true and /bin/false are allowed by OVAL and will be accepted by the scan): install usb-storage /bin/true This will prevent the modprobe program from loading the usb-storage module, but will not prevent an administrator (or another program) from using the insmod program to load the module manually.
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then if LC_ALL=C grep -q -m 1 "^install usb-storage" /etc/modprobe.d/usb-storage.conf ; then sed -i 's#^install usb-storage.*#install usb-storage /bin/false#g' /etc/modprobe.d/usb-storage.conf else echo -e "\n# Disable per security requirements" >> /etc/modprobe.d/usb-storage.conf echo "install usb-storage /bin/false" >> /etc/modprobe.d/usb-storage.conf fi if ! LC_ALL=C grep -q -m 1 "^blacklist usb-storage$" /etc/modprobe.d/usb-storage.conf ; then echo "blacklist usb-storage" >> /etc/modprobe.d/usb-storage.conf fi else >&2 echo 'Remediation is not applicable, nothing was done' fi

review_verdict.feedback: The plan correctly enforces the required modprobe configuration and prevents automatic loading of usb-storage, thereby addressing the vulnerability. concerns: Original file ownership and permissions may not be preserved after editing.
If usb-storage is already loaded, the configuration change will not unload it, leaving the device usable until next reboot.
No backup of /etc/modprobe.d/usb-storage.conf is created before modification, risking accidental loss of prior settings.
Sed command success and error handling are not explicitly checked.
suggested_improvements: Copy the existing /etc/modprobe.d/usb-storage.conf to a backup before editing (e.g., cp -p).
After editing, restore the backup if the sed operation fails.
Preserve file ownership and permissions by recording them before editing and applying them again with chown/chmod.
Check if usb-storage is currently loaded with lsmod and, if so, unload it with modprobe -r usb-storage to ensure immediate enforcement.
Consider running depmod -a if module references have changed.
Add explicit error checking and logging around sed and file operations.

vulnerability.title: Add nosuid Option to /boot/efi
vulnerability.description: The nosuid mount option can be used to prevent execution of setuid programs in /boot/efi. The SUID and SGID permissions should not be required on the boot partition. Add the nosuid option to the fourth column of /etc/fstab for the line which controls mounting of /boot/efi.
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if ( ! ( { rpm --quiet -q kernel-core ;} && { rpm --quiet -q rpm-ostree ;} && { rpm --quiet -q bootc ;} && { ! rpm --quiet -q openshift-kubelet ;} && ([ -f /run/ostree-booted ] || [ -L /ostree ]) ) && ! ( [ -f /.dockerenv ] || [ -f /run/.containerenv ] ) ) && { findmnt --kernel "/boot/efi" > /dev/null || findmnt --fstab "/boot/efi" > /dev/null; }; then function perform_remediation { # the mount point /boot/efi has to be defined in /etc/fstab # before this remediation can be executed. In case it is not defined, the # remediation aborts and no changes regarding the mount point are done. mount_point_match_regexp="$(printf "^[[:space:]]*[^#].*[[:space:]]%s[[:space:]]" "/boot/efi")" grep "$mount_point_match_regexp" -q /etc/fstab \ || { echo

It prevents execution of setuid programs on the EFI partition, which is a common hardening practice and unlikely to cause lockout or system breakage.

vulnerability.title: Add nodev Option to /boot
vulnerability.description: The nodev mount option can be used to prevent device files from being created in /boot. Legitimate character and block devices should exist only in the /dev directory on the root partition or within chroot jails built for system services. Add the nodev option to the fourth column of /etc/fstab for the line which controls mounting of /boot.

( { rpm --quiet -q kernel-core ;} && { rpm --quiet -q rpm-ostree ;} && { rpm --quiet -q bootc ;} && { ! rpm --quiet -q openshift-kubelet ;} && ([ -f /run/ostree-booted ] || [ -L /ostree ]) ) && ! ( [ -f /.dockerenv ] || [ -f /run/.containerenv ] ) ); then function perform_remediation { # the mount point /boot has to be defined in /etc/fstab # before this remediation can be executed. In case it is not defined, the # remediation aborts and no changes regarding the mount point are done. mount_point_match_regexp="$(printf "^[[:space:]]*[^#].*[[:space:]]%s[[:space:]]" "/boot")" grep "$mount_point_match_regexp" -q /etc/fstab \ || { echo "The mount point '/boot' is not even in /etc/fstab, so we can't set up mount options" >&2; echo "Not

review_verdict.feedback: The plan will add the "nodev" option to the /boot entry in /etc/fstab, back up the original file, and immediately remount /boot, effectively resolving the identified vulnerability. The approach is functional and safe, but a few enhancements would make it more robust and align with best-practice hardening procedures.
concerns: The script does not perform a syntax validation of /etc/fstab after modification – a malformed entry could render the system unbootable.
There is no fall‑back mechanism that automatically restores the backup if the edit fails or produces an unusable fstab.
The plan assumes the presence of a /boot entry in /etc/fstab but does not explicitly verify this before editing.
Non‑fatal errors from the ed command (e.g., if it exits with an error status) are not handled; they could leave the file partly modified.
suggested_improvements:
After applying the ed script, run a quick syntax check such as `fstab -c /etc/fstab` or `mount -a -n` to verify the file is still valid; if it fails, restore the backup and exit with an error.  
- Add an explicit check that a /boot mount point exists in /etc/fstab before attempting to edit it, and if not, abort with a clear message.
- Capture the exit status of the ed command and, if it is non‑zero, restore the backup and exit.  
- Optionally, use `sed -i.bak` instead of ed for clearer readability, but keep the atomic nature of the operation.  
- Include a note to notify the operator that a reboot may still be required for full effect on some platforms (e.g., when other services rely on /boot).

side_effects: Possibility of a syntax error in /etc/fstab that could make the system unbootable if the backup is not restored promptly. Remounting /boot with nodev may fail if there are mount options that conflict, potentially leaving /boot unmounted during the operation.

review_verdict.feedback: The plan correctly addresses the vulnerability by ensuring the nosuid option is added to the /boot entry in /etc/fstab and immediately applied via remount. It is safe, idempotent, and includes a backup for recovery. Minor adjustments are needed for maximum reliability.
concerns: The awk command uses -F'\t' which assumes tab-separated fields; many /etc/fstab files use spaces or a mixture of spaces and tabs, so the script may fail to match the /boot line.
The script does not explicitly verify that a /boot entry exists before attempting to replace it; if no entry is found, the fstab remains unchanged and the vulnerability persists.
The remount command uses 'mount -o remount /boot'; if there are other options that need to be preserved, this may not reapply all current options correctly unless they are retained in fstab.
suggested_improvements: Use the default field separator (whitespace) in awk: `awk 'BEGIN{OFS="\t"} $2=="/boot" && !($4 ~ /(^|,)nosuid(,|$)/) { if($4=="") $4="nosuid"; else $4=$4",nosuid" } {print}' /etc/fstab > /tmp/fstab_new`.

vulnerability.title: Add nodev Option to /dev/shm
vulnerability.description: The nodev mount option can be used to prevent creation of device files in /dev/shm. Legitimate character and block devices should not exist within temporary directories like /dev/shm. Add the nodev option to the fourth column of /etc/fstab for the line which controls mounting of /dev/shm.
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if ( ! ( { rpm --quiet -q kernel-core ;} && { rpm --quiet -q rpm-ostree ;} && { rpm --quiet -q bootc ;} && { ! rpm --quiet -q openshift-kubelet ;} && ([ -f /run/ostree-booted ] || [ -L /ostree ]) ) && ! ( [ -f /.dockerenv ] || [ -f /run/.containerenv ] ) ); then function perform_remediation { mount_point_match_regexp="$(printf "^[[:space:]]*[^#].*[[:space:]]%s[[:space:]]" /dev/shm)" # If the mount point is not in /etc/fstab, get previous mount options from /etc/mtab if ! grep -q "$mount_point_match_regexp" /etc/fstab; then # runtime opts without some automatic kernel/userspace-added defaults previous_mount_opts=$(grep "$mount_point_match_regexp" /etc/mtab | head -1 | awk '{print $4}' \ | sed -E "s/(rw|defaults|seclabel|nodev)(,|$)//g;s/

vulnerability.title: Add noexec Option to /dev/shm
vulnerability.description: The noexec mount option can be used to prevent binaries from being executed out of /dev/shm. It can be dangerous to allow the execution of binaries from world-writable temporary storage directories such as /dev/shm. Add the noexec option to the fourth column of /etc/fstab for the line which controls mounting of /dev/shm.

vulnerability.title: Add nosuid Option to /dev/shm
vulnerability.description: The nosuid mount option can be used to prevent execution of setuid programs in /dev/shm. The SUID and SGID permissions should not be required in these world-writable directories. Add the nosuid option to the fourth column of /etc/fstab for the line which controls mounting of /dev/shm.

( { rpm --quiet -q kernel-core ;} && { rpm --quiet -q rpm-ostree ;} && { rpm --quiet -q bootc ;} && { ! rpm --quiet -q openshift-kubelet ;} && ([ -f /run/ostree-booted ] || [ -L /ostree ]) ) && ! ( [ -f /.dockerenv ] || [ -f /run/.containerenv ] ) ); then function perform_remediation { mount_point_match_regexp="$(printf "^[[:space:]]*[^#].*[[:space:]]%s[[:space:]]" /dev/shm)" # If the mount point is not in /etc/fstab, get previous mount options from /etc/mtab if ! grep -q "$mount_point_match_regexp" /etc/fstab; then # runtime opts without some automatic kernel/userspace-added defaults previous_mount_opts=$(grep "$mount_point_match_regexp" /etc/mtab | head -1 | awk '{print $4}' \ | sed -E "s/(rw|defaults|seclabel|nosuid)(,|$)//g;s

review_verdict.feedback: The plan correctly targets the addition of the nosuid option to /dev/shm in /etc/fstab, which will resolve the vulnerability once the mount is refreshed. However, it lacks several best‑practice steps that could reduce risk of accidental misconfiguration.
concerns: Missing backup of /etc/fstab before modification.
No step to remount /dev/shm or notify that a reboot is required to apply the change.
Regular expression or sed command could mis‑parse lines with multiple spaces, comment characters or duplicate /dev/shm entries.
No handling of commented or duplicate /dev/shm entries, risking silent failures or unintended removal of existing options.
suggested_improvements: Create a backup with `cp -p /etc/fstab /etc/fstab.bak` before editing.
After editing fstab, execute `mount -o remount /dev/shm` or instruct that a reboot will apply the change.
Use a more robust pattern that matches only the fourth column and preserves all other columns exactly (e.g., awk-based approach).
Add logic to skip commented lines and to warn or error if multiple active /dev/shm entries exist.

qa_result.verdict_reason: Adding the nosuid option to the /dev/shm entry in /etc/fstab is a standard hardening step that does not require changes to running services. The script’s logic is limited to modifying fstab and does not interfere with sshd, auditd, firewalld, or networking. The only side effect is the need to remount /dev/shm or reboot for the change to take effect, and a very small risk of a malformed fstab line if the regular expression or sed pattern mis‑parses an unusual entry. Overall the remediation will not lock out SSH or break authentication.
side_effects: Requires remount or reboot for change to take effect
Potentially malformed fstab line if regex mis‑parses
No data loss or critical service disruption

vulnerability.title: Add noexec Option to /home
vulnerability.description: The noexec mount option can be used to prevent binaries from being executed out of /home. Add the noexec option to the fourth column of /etc/fstab for the line which controls mounting of /home.
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if ( ! ( { rpm --quiet -q kernel-core ;} && { rpm --quiet -q rpm-ostree ;} && { rpm --quiet -q bootc ;} && { ! rpm --quiet -q openshift-kubelet ;} && ([ -f /run/ostree-booted ] || [ -L /ostree ]) ) && ! ( [ -f /.dockerenv ] || [ -f /run/.containerenv ] ) ); then function perform_remediation { # the mount point /home has to be defined in /etc/fstab # before this remediation can be executed. In case it is not defined, the # remediation aborts and no changes regarding the mount point are done. mount_point_match_regexp="$(printf "^[[:space:]]*[^#].*[[:space:]]%s[[:space:]]" "/home")" grep "$mount_point_match_regexp" -q /etc/fstab \ || { echo "The mount point '/home' is not even in /etc/fstab, so we can't set up mount options" >&2; echo "Not

vulnerability.title: Add nosuid Option to /home
vulnerability.description: The nosuid mount option can be used to prevent execution of setuid programs in /home. The SUID and SGID permissions should not be required in these user data directories. Add the nosuid option to the fourth column of /etc/fstab for the line which controls mounting of /home.

vulnerability.title: Add nodev Option to Non-Root Local Partitions
vulnerability.description: The nodev mount option prevents files from being interpreted as character or block devices. Legitimate character and block devices should exist only in the /dev directory on the root partition or within chroot jails built for system services. Add the nodev option to the fourth column of /etc/fstab for the line which controls mounting of any non-root local partitions.
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if ( ! ( { rpm --quiet -q kernel-core ;} && { rpm --quiet -q rpm-ostree ;} && { rpm --quiet -q bootc ;} && { ! rpm --quiet -q openshift-kubelet ;} && ([ -f /run/ostree-booted ] || [ -L /ostree ]) ) && ! ( [ -f /.dockerenv ] || [ -f /run/.containerenv ] ) ); then MOUNT_OPTION="nodev" # Create array of local non-root partitions readarray -t partitions_records < <(findmnt --mtab --raw --evaluate | grep "^/\w" | grep -v "^/proc" | grep "\s/dev/\w") # Create array of polyinstantiated directories, in case one of them is found in mtab readarray -t polyinstantiated_dirs < \ <(grep -oP "^\s*[^#\s]+\s+\S+" /etc/security/namespace.conf | grep -oP "(?<=\s)\S+?(?=/?\$)") # Define excluded non-local file systems excluded_fstypes=( afs autofs ceph cif

triage.reason: Adding the nodev mount option to non-root local partitions is a standard hardening practice that prevents files from being interpreted as device nodes. It is unlikely to lock out users or break critical services, and the change is confined to the fstab configuration.
triage.estimated_impact: filesystems affected; Potential disruption of services that rely on device files in non-root partitions

vulnerability.title: Disable storing core dumps
vulnerability.description: To set the runtime status of the kernel.core_pattern kernel parameter, run the following command: $ sudo sysctl -w kernel.core_pattern=|/bin/false To make sure that the setting is persistent, add the following line to a file in the directory /etc/sysctl.d: kernel.core_pattern = |/bin/false
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then # Comment out any occurrences of kernel.core_pattern from /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf files for f in /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf /run/sysctl.d/*.conf /usr/local/lib/sysctl.d/*.conf; do # skip systemd-sysctl symlink (/etc/sysctl.d/99-sysctl.conf -> /etc/sysctl.conf) if [[ "$(readlink -f "$f")" == "/etc/sysctl.conf" ]]; then continue; fi matching_list=$(grep -P '^(?!#).*[\s]*kernel.core_pattern.*$' $f | uniq ) if ! test -z "$matching_list"; then while IFS= read -r entry; do escaped_entry=$(sed -e 's|/|\\/|g' <<< "$entry") # comment out "kernel.core_pattern" matches to preserve user data sed -i --follow-symlinks "s/^${escaped_entry}$/# &/g" $f done <<< "$matching_list" fi done # # Set sysctl config file which to save

triage.reason: Setting kernel.core_pattern to |/bin/false is a standard sysctl change that prevents core dumps; it does not affect authentication, networking, or filesystem integrity and is unlikely to cause lockout or system breakage.
triage.estimated_impact: Potential loss of core dump data for debugging

The only consideration is ensuring the sysctl command is properly quoted or escaped to avoid shell parsing errors; the rest of the approach is safe and expected for a hardening change.
side_effects: Potential shell parsing error if the pipe character is not quoted or escaped in the sysctl command

vulnerability.title: Disable Kernel Image Loading
vulnerability.description: To set the runtime status of the kernel.kexec_load_disabled kernel parameter, run the following command: $ sudo sysctl -w kernel.kexec_load_disabled=1 To make sure that the setting is persistent, add the following line to a file in the directory /etc/sysctl.d: kernel.kexec_load_disabled = 1
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then # Comment out any occurrences of kernel.kexec_load_disabled from /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf files for f in /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf /run/sysctl.d/*.conf /usr/local/lib/sysctl.d/*.conf; do # skip systemd-sysctl symlink (/etc/sysctl.d/99-sysctl.conf -> /etc/sysctl.conf) if [[ "$(readlink -f "$f")" == "/etc/sysctl.conf" ]]; then continue; fi matching_list=$(grep -P '^(?!#).*[\s]*kernel.kexec_load_disabled.*$' $f | uniq ) if ! test -z "$matching_list"; then while IFS= read -r entry; do escaped_entry=$(sed -e 's|/|\\/|g' <<< "$entry") # comment out "kernel.kexec_load_disabled" matches to preserve user data sed -i --follow-symlinks "s/^${escaped_entry}$/# &/g" $f done <<< "$matching_list" fi done # # Set sysctl confi

triage.reason: Setting kernel.kexec_load_disabled via sysctl is a standard configuration change that does not affect authentication, networking, or filesystem integrity, and is unlikely to cause lockout or system breakage.
triage.estimated_impact: kernel parameter change

vulnerability.title: Disable Access to Network bpf() Syscall From Unprivileged Processes
vulnerability.description: To set the runtime status of the kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled kernel parameter, run the following command: $ sudo sysctl -w kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled=1 To make sure that the setting is persistent, add the following line to a file in the directory /etc/sysctl.d: kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled = 1
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then # Comment out any occurrences of kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled from /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf files for f in /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf /run/sysctl.d/*.conf /usr/local/lib/sysctl.d/*.conf; do # skip systemd-sysctl symlink (/etc/sysctl.d/99-sysctl.conf -> /etc/sysctl.conf) if [[ "$(readlink -f "$f")" == "/etc/sysctl.conf" ]]; then continue; fi matching_list=$(grep -P '^(?!#).*[\s]*kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled.*$' $f | uniq ) if ! test -z "$matching_list"; then while IFS= read -r entry; do escaped_entry=$(sed -e 's|/|\\/|g' <<< "$entry") # comment out "kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled" matches to preserve user data sed -i --follow-symlinks "s/^${escaped_entry}$/# &/g" $f done <<< "$matching_list" fi done #

vulnerability.title: Restrict usage of ptrace to descendant processes
vulnerability.description: To set the runtime status of the kernel.yama.ptrace_scope kernel parameter, run the following command: $ sudo sysctl -w kernel.yama.ptrace_scope=1 To make sure that the setting is persistent, add the following line to a file in the directory /etc/sysctl.d: kernel.yama.ptrace_scope = 1
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then # Comment out any occurrences of kernel.yama.ptrace_scope from /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf files for f in /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf /run/sysctl.d/*.conf /usr/local/lib/sysctl.d/*.conf; do # skip systemd-sysctl symlink (/etc/sysctl.d/99-sysctl.conf -> /etc/sysctl.conf) if [[ "$(readlink -f "$f")" == "/etc/sysctl.conf" ]]; then continue; fi matching_list=$(grep -P '^(?!#).*[\s]*kernel.yama.ptrace_scope.*$' $f | uniq ) if ! test -z "$matching_list"; then while IFS= read -r entry; do escaped_entry=$(sed -e 's|/|\\/|g' <<< "$entry") # comment out "kernel.yama.ptrace_scope" matches to preserve user data sed -i --follow-symlinks "s/^${escaped_entry}$/# &/g" $f done <<< "$matching_list" fi done # # Set sysctl config file

vulnerability.title: Disable core dump backtraces
vulnerability.description: The ProcessSizeMax option in [Coredump] section of /etc/systemd/coredump.conf or in a drop-in file under /etc/systemd/coredump.conf.d/ specifies the maximum size in bytes of a core which will be processed. Core dumps exceeding this size may be stored, but the backtrace will not be generated.
vulnerability.recommendation:
Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q kernel-core && { rpm --quiet -q systemd; }; then found=false # set value in all files if they contain section or key for f in $(echo -n "/etc/systemd/coredump.conf.d/complianceascode_hardening.conf /etc/systemd/coredump.conf.d/*.conf /etc/systemd/coredump.conf"); do if [ ! -e "$f" ]; then continue fi # find key in section and change value if grep -qzosP "[[:space:]]*\[Coredump\]([^
\[]*
+)+?[[:space:]]*ProcessSizeMax" "$f"; then if ! grep -qPz "ProcessSizeMax=0" "$f"; then sed -i "s/ProcessSizeMax[^(
)]*/ProcessSizeMax=0/" "$f" fi found=true # find section and add key = value to it elif grep -qs "[[:space:]]*\[Coredump\]" "$f"; then sed -i "/[[:space:]]*\[Coredump\]/a ProcessSizeMax=0" "$f" found=true fi done # if s

triage.reason: Setting ProcessSizeMax=0 in systemd coredump configuration is a standard hardening step that prevents backtrace generation for core dumps; it does not affect authentication, networking, or critical services and is unlikely to cause lockout or system breakage.

vulnerability.title: Disable Core Dumps for All Users
vulnerability.description: To disable core dumps for all users, add the following line to /etc/security/limits.conf, or to a file within the /etc/security/limits.d/ directory: * hard core 0
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q kernel-core && { rpm --quiet -q pam; }; then SECURITY_LIMITS_FILE="/etc/security/limits.conf" DROPIN_DIR="/etc/security/limits.d" DROPIN_FILE="$DROPIN_DIR/10-ssg-hardening.conf" REGEX_CORRECT_VALUE="^\s*\*\s+hard\s+core\s+0\s*$" # Remove bad configuration in drop-ins if [ -d "$DROPIN_DIR" ]; then for override in "$DROPIN_DIR"/*.conf; do if [ -f "$override" ] && ! grep -qE "$REGEX_CORRECT_VALUE" "$override"; then sed -ir -E '/^[[:space:]]*\*[[:space:]]+hard[[:space:]]+core[[:space:]]+/ s/^/#/' "$override" fi done fi if [ -d "$DROPIN_DIR" ] && grep -qEr "$REGEX_CORRECT_VALUE" "$DROPIN_DIR"; then exit 0 elif [ ! -d "$DROPIN_DIR" ] && grep -qE "$REGEX_CORRECT_VALUE" "$SECURITY_LIMITS_FILE"; then exit 0 else mkdir -p "$DROP

vulnerability.title: Enable Randomized Layout of Virtual Address Space
vulnerability.description: To set the runtime status of the kernel.randomize_va_space kernel parameter, run the following command: $ sudo sysctl -w kernel.randomize_va_space=2 To make sure that the setting is persistent, add the following line to a file in the directory /etc/sysctl.d: kernel.randomize_va_space = 2
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then # Comment out any occurrences of kernel.randomize_va_space from /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf files for f in /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf /run/sysctl.d/*.conf /usr/local/lib/sysctl.d/*.conf; do # skip systemd-sysctl symlink (/etc/sysctl.d/99-sysctl.conf -> /etc/sysctl.conf) if [[ "$(readlink -f "$f")" == "/etc/sysctl.conf" ]]; then continue; fi matching_list=$(grep -P '^(?!#).*[\s]*kernel.randomize_va_space.*$' $f | uniq ) if ! test -z "$matching_list"; then while IFS= read -r entry; do escaped_entry=$(sed -e 's|/|\\/|g' <<< "$entry") # comment out "kernel.randomize_va_space" matches to preserve user data sed -i --follow-symlinks "s/^${escaped_entry}$/# &/g" $f done <<< "$matching_list" fi done # # Set sysctl config f

vulnerability.title: Enable page allocator poisoning
vulnerability.description: To enable poisoning of free pages, add the argument page_poison=1 to the default GRUB 2 command line for the Linux operating system. To ensure that page_poison=1 is added as a kernel command line argument to newly installed kernels, add page_poison=1 to the default Grub2 command line for Linux operating systems. Modify the line within /etc/default/grub as shown below: GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX="... page_poison=1 ..." Run the following command to update command line for already installed kernels:# grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args="page_poison=1" If the system is distributed as a bootable container image, GRUB2 can't be configured using the method described above, but the following method needs to be used instead. The kernel arguments should be set in /usr/lib/bootc/kargs.d in a TOML file that has the following form: # /usr/lib/bootc/kargs.d/10-example.toml kargs = ["page_poison=1"] For more details on configuring kernel arguments in bootable container images, please refer to Bootc documentation.
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q kernel-core && { rpm --quiet -q grub2-common; }; then if { rpm --quiet -q kernel rpm-ostree bootc && ! rpm --quiet -q openshift-kubelet && { [ -f "/run/.containerenv" ] || [ -f "/.containerenv" ]; }; } ; then KARGS_DIR="/usr/lib/bootc/kargs.d/" if grep -q -E "page_poison" "$KARGS_DIR/*.toml" ; then sed -i -E "s/^(\s*kargs\s*=\s*\[.*)\"page_poison=[^\"]*\"(.*]\s*)/\1\"page_poison=1\"\2/" "$KARGS_DIR/*.toml" else echo "kargs = [\"page_poison=1\"]" >> "$KARGS_DIR/10-page_poison.toml" fi else grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args=page_poison=1 fi else >&2 echo 'Remediation is not applicable, nothing was done' fi

triage.reason: Modifying the GRUB configuration to add a kernel command line argument changes the bootloader settings, which can render the system unbootable if misconfigured. This falls under the policy’s definition of bootloader changes that are considered too dangerous to remediate automatically.
triage.estimated_impact: reboot required; Boot failure; Potential loss of console access; System unbootable

vulnerability.title: Disable KDump Kernel Crash Analyzer (kdump)
vulnerability.description: The kdump service provides a kernel crash dump analyzer. It uses the kexec system call to boot a secondary kernel ("capture" kernel) following a system crash, which can load information from the crashed kernel for analysis. The kdump service can be disabled with the following command: $ sudo systemctl mask --now kdump.service
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then SYSTEMCTL_EXEC='/usr/bin/systemctl' if [[ $("$SYSTEMCTL_EXEC" is-system-running) != "offline" ]]; then "$SYSTEMCTL_EXEC" stop 'kdump.service' fi "$SYSTEMCTL_EXEC" disable 'kdump.service' "$SYSTEMCTL_EXEC" mask 'kdump.service' # Disable socket activation if we have a unit file for it if "$SYSTEMCTL_EXEC" -q list-unit-files kdump.socket; then if [[ $("$SYSTEMCTL_EXEC" is-system-running) != "offline" ]]; then "$SYSTEMCTL_EXEC" stop 'kdump.socket' fi "$SYSTEMCTL_EXEC" mask 'kdump.socket' fi # The service may not be running because it has been started and failed, # so let's reset the state so OVAL checks pass. # Service should be 'inactive', not 'failed' after reboot though. "$SYSTEMCTL_EXEC" reset-failed

triage.reason: Disabling the kdump service is a standard service disable operation that does not affect authentication, networking, or filesystem integrity. It follows typical STIG hardening patterns for service management and is unlikely to cause lockout or system breakage.
triage.estimated_impact: Loss of kernel crash dump data for forensic analysis

qa_result.verdict_reason: Changing /etc/cron.weekly permissions to 0700 restricts access to the root user only, which is the intended owner of cron jobs. Cron daemon runs as root and will still read the files; no critical services such as sshd, auditd, or firewalld are affected. The change may prevent non‑root users from adding or modifying weekly cron jobs, which could affect routine maintenance scripts but does not break core system functionality.
side_effects: Cron jobs located in /etc/cron.weekly may not be executed if they were previously added by non‑root users.

vulnerability.title: Enable the File Access Policy Service
vulnerability.description: The File Access Policy service should be enabled. The fapolicyd service can be enabled with the following command: $ sudo systemctl enable fapolicyd.service
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then SYSTEMCTL_EXEC='/usr/bin/systemctl' "$SYSTEMCTL_EXEC" unmask 'fapolicyd.service' if [[ $("$SYSTEMCTL_EXEC" is-system-running) != "offline" ]]; then "$SYSTEMCTL_EXEC" start 'fapolicyd.service' fi "$SYSTEMCTL_EXEC" enable 'fapolicyd.service' else >&2 echo 'Remediation is not applicable, nothing was done' fi

vulnerability.title: Configure Fapolicy Module to Employ a Deny-all, Permit-by-exception Policy to Allow the Execution of Authorized Software Programs.
vulnerability.description: The Fapolicy module must be configured to employ a deny-all, permit-by-exception policy to allow the execution of authorized software programs and to prevent unauthorized software from running.
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then cat > /etc/fapolicyd/rules.d/99-deny-everything.rules << EOF # Red Hat KCS 7003854 (https://access.redhat.com/solutions/7003854) deny perm=any all : all EOF chmod 644 /etc/fapolicyd/rules.d/99-deny-everything.rules chgrp fapolicyd /etc/fapolicyd/rules.d/99-deny-everything.rules if [ -e "/etc/fapolicyd/fapolicyd.conf" ] ; then LC_ALL=C sed -i "/^\s*permissive\s*=\s*/Id" "/etc/fapolicyd/fapolicyd.conf" else touch "/etc/fapolicyd/fapolicyd.conf" fi # make sure file has newline at the end sed -i -e '$a\' "/etc/fapolicyd/fapolicyd.conf" cp "/etc/fapolicyd/fapolicyd.conf" "/etc/fapolicyd/fapolicyd.conf.bak" # Insert at the end of the file printf '%s\n' "permissive = 0" >> "/etc/fapolicyd/fapolicyd.conf" # C

vulnerability.title: Configure System to Forward All Mail For The Root Account
vulnerability.description: Make sure that mails delivered to root user are forwarded to a monitored email address. Make sure that the address is a valid email address reachable from the system in question. Use the following command to configure the alias: $ sudo echo "root: " >> /etc/aliases $ sudo newaliases
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then var_postfix_root_mail_alias='' # Strip any search characters in the key arg so that the key can be replaced without # adding any search characters to the config file. stripped_key=$(sed 's/[\^=\$,;+]*//g' <<< "^root") # shellcheck disable=SC2059 printf -v formatted_output "%s: %s" "$stripped_key" "$var_postfix_root_mail_alias" # If the key exists, change it. Otherwise, add it to the config_file. # We search for the key string followed by a word boundary (matched by \>), # so if we search for 'setting', 'setting2' won't match. if LC_ALL=C grep -q -m 1 -i -e "^root\\>" "/etc/aliases"; then escaped_formatted_output=$(sed -e 's|/|\\/|g' <<< "$formatted_output") LC_ALL=C sed -i --follow-symlinks "s/^root\\

vulnerability.title: Configure Time Service Maxpoll Interval
vulnerability.description: The maxpoll should be configured to in /etc/ntp.conf or /etc/chrony.conf (or /etc/chrony.d/) to continuously poll time servers. To configure maxpoll in /etc/ntp.conf or /etc/chrony.conf (or /etc/chrony.d/) add the following after each server, pool or peer entry: maxpoll to server directives. If using chrony, any pool directives should be configured too.
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q kernel-core && { ( rpm --quiet -q chrony || rpm --quiet -q ntp ); }; then var_time_service_set_maxpoll='' pof="/usr/sbin/pidof" CONFIG_FILES="/etc/ntp.conf" $pof ntpd || { CHRONY_D_PATH=/etc/chrony.d/ mapfile -t CONFIG_FILES < <(find ${CHRONY_D_PATH}.* -type f -name '*.conf') CONFIG_FILES+=(/etc/chrony.conf) } # get list of ntp files for config_file in "${CONFIG_FILES[@]}" ; do # Set maxpoll values to var_time_service_set_maxpoll sed -i "s/^\(\(server\|pool\|peer\).*maxpoll\) [0-9,-][0-9]*\(.*\)$/\1 $var_time_service_set_maxpoll \3/" "$config_file" done for config_file in "${CONFIG_FILES[@]}" ; do # Add maxpoll to server, pool or peer entries without maxpoll grep "^\(server\|pool\|peer\)" "$config_file" | grep -v maxpo

# Use public servers from the pool.ntp.org project.
# Please consider joining the pool (https://www.pool.ntp.org/join.html).
pool 2.rocky.pool.ntp.org iburst maxpoll 6

# Use NTP servers from DHCP.
sourcedir /run/chrony-dhcp

# Record the rate at which the system clock gains/losses time.
driftfile /var/lib/chrony/drift

# Allow the system clock to be stepped in the first three updates
# if its offset is larger than 1 second.
makestep 1.0 3

# Enable kernel synchronization of the real-time clock (RTC).
rtcsync

# Enable hardware timestamping on all interfaces that support it.
#hwtimestamp *

# Increase the minimum number of selectable sources required to adjust
# the system clock.
#minsources 2

# Allow NTP client access from local network.
#allow 192.168.0.0/16

# Serve time even if not synchronized to a time source.
#local stratum 10

# Require authentication (nts or key option) for all NTP sources.
#authselectmode require

# Specify file containing keys for NTP authentication.
keyfile /etc/chrony.keys

# Save NTS keys and cookies.
ntsdumpdir /var/lib/chrony

# Insert/delete leap seconds by slewing instead of stepping.
#leapsecmode slew

# Get TAI-UTC offset and leap seconds from the system tz database.
leapsectz right/UTC

# Specify directory for log files.
logdir /var/log/chrony

# Select which information is logged.
#log measurements statistics tracking

vulnerability.title: Disable Host-Based Authentication
vulnerability.description: SSH's cryptographic host-based authentication is more secure than .rhosts authentication. However, it is not recommended that hosts unilaterally trust one another, even within an organization. The default SSH configuration disables host-based authentication. The appropriate configuration is used if no value is set for HostbasedAuthentication. To explicitly disable host-based authentication, add or correct the following line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf: HostbasedAuthentication no
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then mkdir -p /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d touch /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-complianceascode-reinforce-os-defaults.conf chmod 0600 /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-complianceascode-reinforce-os-defaults.conf LC_ALL=C sed -i "/^\s*HostbasedAuthentication\s\+/Id" "/etc/ssh/sshd_config" LC_ALL=C sed -i "/^\s*HostbasedAuthentication\s\+/Id" "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d"/*.conf if [ -e "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-complianceascode-reinforce-os-defaults.conf" ] ; then LC_ALL=C sed -i "/^\s*HostbasedAuthentication\s\+/Id" "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-complianceascode-reinforce-os-defaults.conf" else touch "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-complianceascode-reinforce-os-defaults.conf" fi # make sure file has newline at the end sed -i -e '$a\' "

vulnerability.title: Disable Compression Or Set Compression to delayed
vulnerability.description: Compression is useful for slow network connections over long distances but can cause performance issues on local LANs. If use of compression is required, it should be enabled only after a user has authenticated; otherwise, it should be disabled. To disable compression or delay compression until after a user has successfully authenticated, add or correct the following line in the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file: Compression
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then var_sshd_disable_compression='' mkdir -p /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d touch /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf chmod 0600 /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf LC_ALL=C sed -i "/^\s*Compression\s\+/Id" "/etc/ssh/sshd_config" LC_ALL=C sed -i "/^\s*Compression\s\+/Id" "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d"/*.conf if [ -e "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf" ] ; then LC_ALL=C sed -i "/^\s*Compression\s\+/Id" "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf" else touch "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf" fi # make sure file has newline at the end sed -i -e '$a\' "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf" cp "/

vulnerability.title: Disable GSSAPI Authentication
vulnerability.description: Unless needed, SSH should not permit extraneous or unnecessary authentication mechanisms like GSSAPI. The default SSH configuration disallows authentications based on GSSAPI. The appropriate configuration is used if no value is set for GSSAPIAuthentication. To explicitly disable GSSAPI authentication, add or correct the following line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf: GSSAPIAuthentication no

vulnerability.title: Disable SSH Support for .rhosts Files
vulnerability.description: SSH can emulate the behavior of the obsolete rsh command in allowing users to enable insecure access to their accounts via .rhosts files. The default SSH configuration disables support for .rhosts. The appropriate configuration is used if no value is set for IgnoreRhosts. To explicitly disable support for .rhosts files, add or correct the following line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf: IgnoreRhosts yes
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then mkdir -p /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d touch /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-complianceascode-reinforce-os-defaults.conf chmod 0600 /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-complianceascode-reinforce-os-defaults.conf LC_ALL=C sed -i "/^\s*IgnoreRhosts\s\+/Id" "/etc/ssh/sshd_config" LC_ALL=C sed -i "/^\s*IgnoreRhosts\s\+/Id" "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d"/*.conf if [ -e "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-complianceascode-reinforce-os-defaults.conf" ] ; then LC_ALL=C sed -i "/^\s*IgnoreRhosts\s\+/Id" "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-complianceascode-reinforce-os-defaults.conf" else touch "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-complianceascode-reinforce-os-defaults.conf" fi # make sure file has newline at the end sed -i -e '$a\' "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-complia

triage.reason: Disabling IgnoreRhosts is a standard SSH hardening step that does not risk lockout or system breakage.

vulnerability.title: Disable SSH Support for User Known Hosts
vulnerability.description: SSH can allow system users to connect to systems if a cache of the remote systems public keys is available. This should be disabled. To ensure this behavior is disabled, add or correct the following line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf: IgnoreUserKnownHosts yes

review_verdict.feedback: The plan correctly implements the required IgnoreUserKnownHosts yes directive, cleans conflicting entries, verifies syntax, and reloads sshd. It is acceptable for remediation but can be tightened to avoid edge‑case failures and to follow best practices more rigorously.
concerns: Backup of *.conf files uses a single cp command that will fail if the directory contains no .conf files or has many files; it also does not preserve original filenames.
The sed removal pattern deletes any line starting with optional ‘#’ but may also delete lines that are intentionally commented out elsewhere; a more targeted regexp could be safer.

The plan does not explicitly chown root:root for the newly created 00‑complianceascode‑hardening.conf file, which could leave it with a non‑root owner if run under sudo with a different effective user.
The inclusion of the /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d directory into the main sshd_config is mentioned but not shown in concrete commands; if the Include line is missing, the directive will have no effect.
Ensuring a trailing newline in the new file is stated but not executed; a missing newline may cause parsing issues on some SSHD versions.
suggested_improvements: Use a loop or nullglob to back up each existing *.conf file individually rather than a single cp command; e.g., for f in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf; do [ -e "$f" ] && cp "$f" "$f.bak"; done

qa_result.verdict_reason: The remediation plan correctly ensures the IgnoreUserKnownHosts setting is enforced in a dedicated, override‑friendly configuration file, validates sshd syntax before reload, and preserves existing configurations through backups. Potential minor issues with backup naming or accidental deletion of similarly named comments are low‑impact and unlikely to cause service interruption. No critical services other than sshd are affected beyond a safe reload.
side_effects: Backup filenames for *.conf may not preserve original names if using a single cp command; potential accidental removal of comment lines containing the string; the new hardening file may inherit an unexpected ownership if run under a non‑root user.

vulnerability.title: Do Not Allow SSH Environment Options
vulnerability.description: Ensure that users are not able to override environment variables of the SSH daemon. The default SSH configuration disables environment processing. The appropriate configuration is used if no value is set for PermitUserEnvironment. To explicitly disable Environment options, add or correct the following /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf: PermitUserEnvironment no

vulnerability.title: Enable Use of Strict Mode Checking
vulnerability.description: SSHs StrictModes option checks file and ownership permissions in the user's home directory .ssh folder before accepting login. If world- writable permissions are found, logon is rejected. The default SSH configuration has StrictModes enabled. The appropriate configuration is used if no value is set for StrictModes. To explicitly enable StrictModes in SSH, add or correct the following line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf: StrictModes yes
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then mkdir -p /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d touch /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-complianceascode-reinforce-os-defaults.conf chmod 0600 /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-complianceascode-reinforce-os-defaults.conf LC_ALL=C sed -i "/^\s*StrictModes\s\+/Id" "/etc/ssh/sshd_config" LC_ALL=C sed -i "/^\s*StrictModes\s\+/Id" "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d"/*.conf if [ -e "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-complianceascode-reinforce-os-defaults.conf" ] ; then LC_ALL=C sed -i "/^\s*StrictModes\s\+/Id" "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-complianceascode-reinforce-os-defaults.conf" else touch "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-complianceascode-reinforce-os-defaults.conf" fi # make sure file has newline at the end sed -i -e '$a\' "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-compliance

triage.reason: Enabling StrictModes is a standard SSH configuration change that is already the default; it does not risk lockout or system breakage.

vulnerability.title: Enable SSH Print Last Log
vulnerability.description: Ensure that SSH will display the date and time of the last successful account logon. The default SSH configuration enables print of the date and time of the last login. The appropriate configuration is used if no value is set for PrintLastLog. To explicitly enable LastLog in SSH, add or correct the following line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf: PrintLastLog yes
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then mkdir -p /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d touch /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-complianceascode-reinforce-os-defaults.conf chmod 0600 /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-complianceascode-reinforce-os-defaults.conf LC_ALL=C sed -i "/^\s*PrintLastLog\s\+/Id" "/etc/ssh/sshd_config" LC_ALL=C sed -i "/^\s*PrintLastLog\s\+/Id" "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d"/*.conf if [ -e "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-complianceascode-reinforce-os-defaults.conf" ] ; then LC_ALL=C sed -i "/^\s*PrintLastLog\s\+/Id" "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-complianceascode-reinforce-os-defaults.conf" else touch "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-complianceascode-reinforce-os-defaults.conf" fi # make sure file has newline at the end sed -i -e '$a\' "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-complia

triage.reason: Enabling PrintLastLog is a standard SSH configuration change that does not affect authentication flow or system stability; it simply displays the last login time.

vulnerability.title: Force frequent session key renegotiation
vulnerability.description: The RekeyLimit parameter specifies how often the session key of the is renegotiated, both in terms of amount of data that may be transmitted and the time elapsed. To decrease the default limits, add or correct the following line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf: RekeyLimit
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then var_rekey_limit_size='' var_rekey_limit_time='' mkdir -p /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d touch /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf chmod 0600 /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf LC_ALL=C sed -i "/^\s*RekeyLimit\s\+/Id" "/etc/ssh/sshd_config" LC_ALL=C sed -i "/^\s*RekeyLimit\s\+/Id" "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d"/*.conf if [ -e "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf" ] ; then LC_ALL=C sed -i "/^\s*RekeyLimit\s\+/Id" "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf" else touch "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf" fi # make sure file has newline at the end sed -i -e '$a\' "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardenin

vulnerability.title: Set SSH Daemon LogLevel to VERBOSE
vulnerability.description: The VERBOSE parameter configures the SSH daemon to record login and logout activity. To specify the log level in SSH, add or correct the following line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf: LogLevel VERBOSE
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then mkdir -p /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d touch /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf chmod 0600 /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf LC_ALL=C sed -i "/^\s*LogLevel\s\+/Id" "/etc/ssh/sshd_config" LC_ALL=C sed -i "/^\s*LogLevel\s\+/Id" "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d"/*.conf if [ -e "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf" ] ; then LC_ALL=C sed -i "/^\s*LogLevel\s\+/Id" "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf" else touch "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf" fi # make sure file has newline at the end sed -i -e '$a\' "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode-hardening.conf" cp "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-complianceascode

triage.reason: Setting LogLevel to VERBOSE is a standard SSH configuration change that only increases logging verbosity and does not affect authentication or service availability. It follows STIG hardening patterns and poses no risk of lockout or system breakage.

**Remediation Summary**

1. **Determine the auditd rule source**
   * The presence of the comment  
     `## This file is automatically generated from /etc/audit/rules.d`  
     in `/etc/audit/audit.rules` shows that the system uses **augenrules** (i.e., rules are read from files in `/etc/audit/rules.d`).

2. **Ensure the rule file exists and contains the required watch**
   * Path: `/etc/audit/rules.d/cronjobs.rules`
   * Expected line:  
     ```
     -w /etc/cron.d/ -p wa -k cronjobs
     ```
   * Actions:
     * If the file **does not exist**, create it and add the rule line.
     * If the file **exists** but the rule line is missing, append it.
     * Do **not** replace any other existing rules in that file.

3. **Set correct ownership and permissions**
   * Owner/Group: `root:root`
   * Mode: `0640`

4. **Reload the audit daemon to apply changes**
   * Because the system uses augenrules, restarting the service will cause auditd to reread the rules.
   * Command: `systemctl restart auditd`

---

**Applied Actions**

| Step | Tool | Command / Payload |
|------|------|-------------------|
| 1 | `read_file` | `/etc/audit/rules.d/cronjobs.rules` (detected missing) |
| 2 | `write_file` | Create `/etc/audit/rules.d/cronjobs.rules` with line `-w /etc/cron.d/ -p wa -k cronjobs` and mode `0640`. |
| 3 | `run_cmd` | `chown root:root /etc/audit/rules.d/cronjobs.rules` |
| 4 | `run_cmd` | `systemctl restart auditd` |

> All commands were executed individually, respecting the “one command per run_cmd” rule. No duplicate lines were added; the new rule was appended (or created if absent). The audit daemon was restarted so the new rule becomes active immediately.

**Outcome**

The `/etc/cron.d/` directory is now being monitored for write and attribute changes by auditd, fulfilling the STIG requirement **audit_rules_etc_cron_d**. The system remains operational, with no impact on SSH, networking, or other services.

concerns: If the script blindly overwrites /etc/audit/rules.d/cronjobs.rules when it already exists, other custom rules could be lost.  The plan should append or merge, not replace, the rule.  The order of the rule in the file could affect prematching of audit rules if other error‑handling rules rely on ordering.
suggested_improvements: Use a conditional check that appends the rule only if it does not already exist, or merge lines intelligently.  Explicitly set the file mode to 0640 and ownership to root:root after creation.  Consider validating the syntax of the existing audit file before modification.  Include a fallback to use `auditctl -R /etc/audit/rules.d/cronjobs.rules` after reload if the system prefers `auditctl` over `augenrules`.  Log the change to a secure audit log for operational visibility.

qa_result.verdict_reason: The remediation correctly adds a watch on /etc/cron.d/ for write and attribute changes, reloads auditd to apply the rule, and preserves permissions/ownership. It does not modify services like sshd, firewalld, or networking and only targets auditd, a separate daemon. Overwriting an existing rules file could lose other custom rules, but this is a conservative side effect that does not disrupt critical services. Overall, the plan is correct and unlikely to cause outages.
side_effects: If the script overwrites an existing /etc/audit/rules.d/cronjobs.rules file that contains other custom audit rules, those rules will be lost or duplicated. A reload of auditd may briefly suspend audit logging until the daemon restarts.

vulnerability.title: Make the auditd Configuration Immutable
vulnerability.description: If the auditd daemon is configured to use the augenrules program to read audit rules during daemon startup (the default), add the following line to a file with suffix .rules in the directory /etc/audit/rules.d in order to make the auditd configuration immutable: -e 2 If the auditd daemon is configured to use the auditctl utility to read audit rules during daemon startup, add the following line to /etc/audit/audit.rules file in order to make the auditd configuration immutable: -e 2 With this setting, a reboot will be required to change any audit rules.
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q audit && rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then # Traverse all of: # # /etc/audit/audit.rules, (for auditctl case) # /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules (for augenrules case) # # files to check if '-e .*' setting is present in that '*.rules' file already. # If found, delete such occurrence since auditctl(8) manual page instructs the # '-e 2' rule should be placed as the last rule in the configuration find /etc/audit /etc/audit/rules.d -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*.rules' -exec sed -i '/-e[[:space:]]\+.*/d' {} ';' # Append '-e 2' requirement at the end of both: # * /etc/audit/audit.rules file (for auditctl case) # * /etc/audit/rules.d/immutable.rules (for augenrules case) for AUDIT_FILE in "/etc/audit/audit.rules" "/etc/audit/rules.d/i

triage.reason: Adding the immutable flag (-e 2) to auditd rules is a standard STIG hardening step that does not affect authentication, networking, or filesystem operation and only requires a reboot to take effect.
triage.estimated_impact: reboot required

vulnerability.title: Ensure auditd Collects System Administrator Actions - /etc/sudoers
vulnerability.description: At a minimum, the audit system should collect administrator actions for all users and root. If the auditd daemon is configured to use the augenrules program to read audit rules during daemon startup (the default), add the following lines to a file with suffix .rules in the directory /etc/audit/rules.d: -w /etc/sudoers -p wa -k actions If the auditd daemon is configured to use the auditctl utility to read audit rules during daemon startup, add the following lines to /etc/audit/audit.rules: -w /etc/sudoers -p wa -k actions
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q audit && rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then # Perform the remediation for both possible tools: 'auditctl' and 'augenrules' # Create a list of audit *.rules files that should be inspected for presence and correctness # of a particular audit rule. The scheme is as follows: # # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Tool used to load audit rules | Rule already defined | Audit rules file to inspect | # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # auditctl | Doesn't matter | /etc/audit/audit.rules | # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # augenrules | Yes | /etc/audit/rules.

triage.reason: Adding an audit rule for /etc/sudoers is a standard STIG hardening step that does not affect system operation or access. It simply enables logging of sudo activity and follows the recommended pattern for audit rule configuration.
triage.estimated_impact: authentication/authorization affected; Potential for missing audit logs if rule is incorrectly configured

vulnerability.title: Ensure auditd Collects System Administrator Actions - /etc/sudoers.d/
vulnerability.description: At a minimum, the audit system should collect administrator actions for all users and root. If the auditd daemon is configured to use the augenrules program to read audit rules during daemon startup (the default), add the following lines to a file with suffix .rules in the directory /etc/audit/rules.d: -w /etc/sudoers.d/ -p wa -k actions If the auditd daemon is configured to use the auditctl utility to read audit rules during daemon startup, add the following lines to /etc/audit/audit.rules: -w /etc/sudoers.d/ -p wa -k actions
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q audit && rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then # Perform the remediation for both possible tools: 'auditctl' and 'augenrules' # Create a list of audit *.rules files that should be inspected for presence and correctness # of a particular audit rule. The scheme is as follows: # # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Tool used to load audit rules | Rule already defined | Audit rules file to inspect | # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # auditctl | Doesn't matter | /etc/audit/audit.rules | # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # augenrules | Yes | /etc/audit/rules.

llm_verdict.message:
**Planned remediation steps**

1. **Create the rules directory (if necessary)**  
   • `mkdir -p /etc/audit/rules.d`  

2. **Ensure the augenrules file /etc/audit/rules.d/sudoers.rules exists**  
   • Read `/etc/audit/rules.d/sudoers.rules`.  
   • If it does not exist, create it with empty content.  

3. **Add the required rule to /etc/audit/rules.d/sudoers.rules**  
   • Read the current contents.  
   • If the line `-w /etc/sudoers.d/ -p wa -k actions` is missing, append it.  

4. **Set correct ownership and mode for the augenrules file**  
   • `chown root:root /etc/audit/rules.d/sudoers.rules`  
   • `chmod 0644 /etc/audit/rules.d/sudoers.rules`  

5. **If /etc/audit/audit.rules exists, ensure the rule is present there too**  
   • Read `/etc/audit/audit.rules`.  
   • If missing, append the same rule.  
   • `auditctl -R /etc/audit/audit.rules` to apply the change immediately.  

6. **Reload auditd to make sure all rules are active**  
   • `systemctl restart auditd`  

**Rationale**

* The rule must be present in the augenrules directory (the default loader) and, if auditd is started with `auditctl`, in `/etc/audit/audit.rules`.  
* Ownership and mode are set to the expected defaults (root:root, 0644).  
* The audit daemon is restarted at the end to ensure the new rule takes effect.  

**Execution plan** (one command at a time, with `read_file` before modifications)

1. `run_cmd` – `mkdir -p /etc/audit/rules.d`  
2. `read_file` – `/etc/audit/rules.d/sudoers.rules`  
3. If not found → `write_file` – `/etc/audit/rules.d/sudoers.rules` with empty content  
4. `read_file` – `/etc/audit/rules.d/sudoers.rules`  
5. If rule missing → `write_file` – `/etc/audit/rules.d/sudoers.rules` with appended rule line  
6. `run_cmd` – `chown root:root /etc/audit/rules.d/sudoers.rules`  
7. `run_cmd` – `chmod 0644 /etc/audit/rules.d/sudoers.rules`  
8. `read_file` – `/etc/audit/audit.rules` (if file exists)  
9. If rule missing → `write_file` – `/etc/audit/audit.rules` with appended rule line  
10. `run_cmd` – `auditctl -R /etc/audit/audit.rules` (only if file existed)  
11. `run_cmd` – `systemctl restart auditd`  

This sequence guarantees the audit rule is added correctly, avoids duplications, applies to both augenrules and auditctl loading mechanisms, and reloads the audit daemon to apply the change immediately.

**Planned remediation steps**

1. **Create the rules directory (if necessary)**  
   • `mkdir -p /etc/audit/rules.d`  

2. **Ensure the augenrules file /etc/audit/rules.d/sudoers.rules exists**  
   • Read `/etc/audit/rules.d/sudoers.rules`.  
   • If it does not exist, create it with empty content.  

3. **Add the required rule to /etc/audit/rules.d/sudoers.rules**  
   • Read the current contents.  
   • If the line `-w /etc/sudoers.d/ -p wa -k actions` is missing, append it.  

4. **Set correct ownership and mode for the augenrules file**  
   • `chown root:root /etc/audit/rules.d/sudoers.rules`  
   • `chmod 0644 /etc/audit/rules.d/sudoers.rules`  

5. **If /etc/audit/audit.rules exists, ensure the rule is present there too**  
   • Read `/etc/audit/audit.rules`.  
   • If missing, append the same rule.  
   • `auditctl -R /etc/audit/audit.rules` to apply the change immediately.  

6. **Reload auditd to make sure all rules are active**  
   • `systemctl restart auditd`  

**Rationale**

* The rule must be present in the augenrules directory (the default loader) and, if auditd is started with `auditctl`, in `/etc/audit/audit.rules`.  
* Ownership and mode are set to the expected defaults (root:root, 0644).  
* The audit daemon is restarted at the end to ensure the new rule takes effect.  

**Execution plan** (one command at a time, with `read_file` before modifications)

1. `run_cmd` – `mkdir -p /etc/audit/rules.d`  
2. `read_file` – `/etc/audit/rules.d/sudoers.rules`  
3. If not found → `write_file` – `/etc/audit/rules.d/sudoers.rules` with empty content  
4. `read_file` – `/etc/audit/rules.d/sudoers.rules`  
5. If rule missing → `write_file` – `/etc/audit/rules.d/sudoers.rules` with appended rule line  
6. `run_cmd` – `chown root:root /etc/audit/rules.d/sudoers.rules`

10. `run_cmd` – `auditctl -R /etc/audit/audit.rules` (only if file existed)  
11. `run_cmd` – `systemctl restart auditd`  

This sequence guarantees the audit rule is added correctly, avoids duplications, applies to both augenrules and auditctl loading mechanisms, and reloads the audit daemon to apply the change immediately.

review_verdict.feedback: The plan correctly adds the audit rule in both possible loader configurations, uses idempotent checks, sets appropriate permissions, and reloads auditd to apply changes. Minor refinements are suggested to improve detection robustness and clarification of file manipulation commands.
concerns: Detection logic may misidentify the loader if /etc/audit/rules.d exists but contains no .rules files; this could lead to applying the rule to the wrong file.
The plan references abstract functions like read_file/write_file and run_cmd; concrete shell commands would improve clarity.
The rule string is hard‑coded; if audit policy requires a different action mask (e.g., -p wa), the plan needs update time.
Reload sequence uses 'augenrules --load && systemctl restart auditd'; if augenrules fails to load, the restart may still occur, potentially leaving the system with stale rules.

No explicit check that /etc/audit/rules.d directory and /etc/audit/audit.rules file have correct ownership/permissions before writing; the plan sets them after writing but missing pre‑existing state check.
suggested_improvements: Replace loader detection with a deterministic check explicitly querying auditctl configuration, such as inspecting /etc/audit/audit.rules for the presence of 'augenrules' or testing the outcome of 'augenrules --load' before deciding.
Use `tee -a` or `echo` to append the rule directly instead of abstract read/write functions, ensuring line breaks and formatting are preserved.
Add a fall‑back step to apply the rule to both files if the loader is ambiguous, ensuring coverage across distributions.
Include an explicit `systemctl is-active auditd.service` check before restarting to avoid unnecessary service restarts when auditd is down.
Document handling of existing lines that may be commented out or have different whitespace, using `grep -Fx` or `sed -i` to uncomment or replace to avoid duplicates.

It performs idempotent checks, preserves existing rules, ownership and permissions, and reloads auditd in a manner that will not disrupt critical services. The only minor risk is a brief auditd restart and potential mis‑detection of the loader when no .rules files are present, which would simply result in the rule not being loaded rather than any system breakage. Overall the plan addresses the vulnerability without causing service outages or lockouts.
side_effects: Brief auditd restart may pause logging temporarily.
If /etc/audit/rules.d exists but contains no .rules files, the script may incorrectly assume auditctl loader and the added rule will not be applied in an augenrules environment.

vulnerability.title: Record Events When Privileged Executables Are Run
vulnerability.description: Verify the system generates an audit record when privileged functions are executed. If audit is using the "auditctl" tool to load the rules, run the following command: $ sudo grep execve /etc/audit/audit.rules If audit is using the "augenrules" tool to load the rules, run the following command: $ sudo grep -r execve /etc/audit/rules.d -a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S execve -C uid!=euid -F euid=0 -k setuid -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve -C uid!=euid -F euid=0 -k setuid -a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S execve -C gid!=egid -F egid=0 -k setgid -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve -C gid!=egid -F egid=0 -k setgid If both the "b32" and "b64" audit rules for "SUID" files are not defined, this is a finding. If both the "b32" and "b64" audit rules for "SGID" files are not defined, this is a finding.
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q audit && rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then # First perform the remediation of the syscall rule # Retrieve hardware architecture of the underlying system [ "$(getconf LONG_BIT)" = "32" ] && RULE_ARCHS=("b32") || RULE_ARCHS=("b32" "b64") for ARCH in "${RULE_ARCHS[@]}" do ACTION_ARCH_FILTERS="-a always,exit -F arch=$ARCH" OTHER_FILTERS="-C uid!=euid -F euid=0" AUID_FILTERS="" SYSCALL="execve" KEY="setuid" SYSCALL_GROUPING="" # Perform the remediation for both possible tools: 'auditctl' and 'augenrules' unset syscall_a unset syscall_grouping unset syscall_string unset syscall unset file_to_edit unset rule_to_edit unset rule_syscalls_to_edit unset other_string unset auid_string unset full_rule # Load macro arguments into arr

vulnerability.title: Shutdown System When Auditing Failures Occur
vulnerability.description: If the auditd daemon is configured to use the augenrules program to read audit rules during daemon startup (the default), add the following line to to the bottom of a file with suffix .rules in the directory /etc/audit/rules.d: -f If the auditd daemon is configured to use the auditctl utility to read audit rules during daemon startup, add the following line to the bottom of the /etc/audit/audit.rules file: -f
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q audit && rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then var_audit_failure_mode='' # Traverse all of: # # /etc/audit/audit.rules, (for auditctl case) # /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules (for augenrules case) find /etc/audit /etc/audit/rules.d -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*.rules' -exec sed -i '/-f[[:space:]]\+.*/d' {} ';' for AUDIT_FILE in "/etc/audit/audit.rules" "/etc/audit/rules.d/immutable.rules" do echo '' >> $AUDIT_FILE echo '# Set the audit.rules configuration to halt system upon audit failure per security requirements' >> $AUDIT_FILE echo "-f $var_audit_failure_mode" >> $AUDIT_FILE done else >&2 echo 'Remediation is not applicable, nothing was done' fi

vulnerability.title: Record Events that Modify User/Group Information - /etc/group
vulnerability.description: If the auditd daemon is configured to use the augenrules program to read audit rules during daemon startup (the default), add the following lines to a file with suffix .rules in the directory /etc/audit/rules.d: -w /etc/group -p wa -k audit_rules_usergroup_modification If the auditd daemon is configured to use the auditctl utility to read audit rules during daemon startup, add the following lines to /etc/audit/audit.rules: -w /etc/group -p wa -k audit_rules_usergroup_modification
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q audit && rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then # Perform the remediation for both possible tools: 'auditctl' and 'augenrules' # Create a list of audit *.rules files that should be inspected for presence and correctness # of a particular audit rule. The scheme is as follows: # # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Tool used to load audit rules | Rule already defined | Audit rules file to inspect | # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # auditctl | Doesn't matter | /etc/audit/audit.rules | # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # augenrules | Yes | /etc/audit/rules.

triage.reason: Adding an audit rule to monitor changes to /etc/group is a standard configuration change that does not affect authentication, networking, or filesystem operation. It follows STIG hardening patterns for audit rules and carries no risk of service lockout or system breakage.

review_verdict.feedback: The plan will correctly add the required audit rule and reload auditd, effectively addressing the vulnerability. It follows a clear read-modify-write sequence and maintains appropriate permissions.
concerns:
The plan only targets augenrules; systems that rely solely on auditctl and do not process /etc/audit/rules.d files will not have the rule applied.  
Overwriting an existing .rules file could inadvertently remove other relevant audit rules if the file is shared.  
No explicit validation that the rule syntax is correct or that no duplicate entries exist.  
The plan does not account for potential SELinux contexts on the rule file.
suggested_improvements:
Check if the system is configured to use auditctl directly; if so, also append the rule to /etc/audit/audit.rules or switch to using augenrules.  
When writing the rule file, preserve existing content by appending the line rather than overwriting, or create a dedicated rule file that solely contains this rule to avoid accidental loss of other rules.  
Add a simple syntax validation step (e.g., grep for the exact pattern) before appending to prevent malformed entries.  
Set the correct SELinux context for the new rules file (e.g., restorecon), if SELinux is enforcing.

qa_result.verdict_reason: The plan correctly adds the required audit rule for /etc/group monitoring and restarts auditd to apply the change. Restarting auditd is a normal operation that will not lock out SSH or other services. The only noteworthy side effect is that if the target .rules file already existed and contained other audit rules, those rules would be lost because the file is overwritten rather than merged. This does not cause service outages but could reduce audit coverage.
side_effects: Overwriting an existing .rules file may remove other audit rules that were previously defined in that file, potentially reducing audit coverage.

vulnerability.title: Record Events that Modify User/Group Information - /etc/gshadow
vulnerability.description: If the auditd daemon is configured to use the augenrules program to read audit rules during daemon startup (the default), add the following lines to a file with suffix .rules in the directory /etc/audit/rules.d: -w /etc/gshadow -p wa -k audit_rules_usergroup_modification If the auditd daemon is configured to use the auditctl utility to read audit rules during daemon startup, add the following lines to /etc/audit/audit.rules: -w /etc/gshadow -p wa -k audit_rules_usergroup_modification
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q audit && rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then # Perform the remediation for both possible tools: 'auditctl' and 'augenrules' # Create a list of audit *.rules files that should be inspected for presence and correctness # of a particular audit rule. The scheme is as follows: # # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Tool used to load audit rules | Rule already defined | Audit rules file to inspect | # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # auditctl | Doesn't matter | /etc/audit/audit.rules | # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # augenrules | Yes | /etc/audit/rules.

vulnerability.title: Record Events that Modify User/Group Information - /etc/security/opasswd
vulnerability.description: If the auditd daemon is configured to use the augenrules program to read audit rules during daemon startup (the default), add the following lines to a file with suffix .rules in the directory /etc/audit/rules.d: -w /etc/security/opasswd -p wa -k audit_rules_usergroup_modification If the auditd daemon is configured to use the auditctl utility to read audit rules during daemon startup, add the following lines to /etc/audit/audit.rules: -w /etc/security/opasswd -p wa -k audit_rules_usergroup_modification
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q audit && rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then # Perform the remediation for both possible tools: 'auditctl' and 'augenrules' # Create a list of audit *.rules files that should be inspected for presence and correctness # of a particular audit rule. The scheme is as follows: # # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Tool used to load audit rules | Rule already defined | Audit rules file to inspect | # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # auditctl | Doesn't matter | /etc/audit/audit.rules | # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # augenrules | Yes | /etc/audit/rules.

vulnerability.title: Record Events that Modify User/Group Information - /etc/passwd
vulnerability.description: If the auditd daemon is configured to use the augenrules program to read audit rules during daemon startup (the default), add the following lines to a file with suffix .rules in the directory /etc/audit/rules.d: -w /etc/passwd -p wa -k audit_rules_usergroup_modification If the auditd daemon is configured to use the auditctl utility to read audit rules during daemon startup, add the following lines to /etc/audit/audit.rules: -w /etc/passwd -p wa -k audit_rules_usergroup_modification
vulnerability.recommendation: Remediation script: # Remediation is applicable only in certain platforms if rpm --quiet -q audit && rpm --quiet -q kernel-core; then # Perform the remediation for both possible tools: 'auditctl' and 'augenrules' # Create a list of audit *.rules files that should be inspected for presence and correctness # of a particular audit rule. The scheme is as follows: # # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Tool used to load audit rules | Rule already defined | Audit rules file to inspect | # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # auditctl | Doesn't matter | /etc/audit/audit.rules | # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # augenrules | Yes | /etc/audit/rules.

llm_verdict.message:
**Remediation Summary**

| File | Action | Result |
|------|--------|--------|
| `/etc/audit/rules.d/10-passwd.rules` | Created with the rule to monitor `/etc/passwd` | `-w /etc/passwd -p wa -k audit_rules_usergroup_modification` (permissions `0640`, owner `root:root`) |
| `/etc/audit/audit.rules` | Appended the same rule after the autogenerated block | Rule added at the end of the file |
| Audit daemon | Applied the new rule via `auditctl` | Rule active without needing a service restart (unit refuses `reload`/`restart`) |

**What was done**

1. Created/overwrote the file **`/etc/audit/rules.d/10-passwd.rules`** with the required audit rule.
2. Appended the rule to **`/etc/audit/audit.rules`** to cover auditd installations that load rules directly via `auditctl`.
3. Loaded the new rule set into auditd with:  
   ```bash
   auditctl -R /etc/audit/audit.rules
   ```
   (The service does not support `reload` or `restart`; the manual load applies the rule immediately.)

**Verification**

* No duplicate rule lines were added.
* Permission set to `0640` with owner `root:root` for both files.
* The new rule is present in both the augenrules rule directory and the auditctl rule file, satisfying the STIG requirement.

The system should now record all modifications to `/etc/passwd`.
